verdict.plain: This policy makes a serious attempt to boost social and affordable housing through new funding, stronger planning rules, and Right to Buy reforms — but even on optimistic projections it only partially closes the gap between supply and need, and delivery risks remain real.
verdict.biggest_unknown: Whether the £39bn Social and Affordable Homes Programme will actually deliver 300,000 homes at the promised social-rent mix, given cost-minimisation pressures and historical planning system shortfalls.

verdict.rationale: The policy attacks the affordable housing crisis on multiple fronts: a large new funding programme (£39bn SAHP), stronger planning obligations, Right to Buy reform, and capacity support for councils and housing associations. The baseline evidence shows a desperate need — the worst affordable-homes ratio on record, 1.27 million on waiting lists, and a decade in which only 14% of new affordable homes were social rent. The policy's direction of travel on all these fronts is clearly positive. The SAHP's 60% social-rent target is a meaningful shift from recent practice. RTB reforms — particularly the 35-year new-build exemption and sharply reduced discounts — should slow the haemorrhage of stock. These are genuine, substantive measures. However, the magnitude must be kept honest. The Resolution Foundation projects the SAHP would lift the affordable-homes ratio only marginally (88 to 91 per 1,000 adults), well below the consensus need of 90,000 social homes per year. Delivering even 30,000 social homes annually (60% of 50,000 SAHP homes per year) leaves a large gap. Cost-minimisation pressures in grant allocation and tenure-blind planning approvals could erode the social-rent mix in practice. RTB abolition advocates argue the reforms do not go far enough. On balance, the evidence supports a 'moderate' improvement verdict: the policy is a genuine, substantive step up — likely the most significant in a generation — but structural constraints mean it will not resolve the affordable housing crisis within this parliament, and effects will accumulate only over the long term.

verifier.notes: All claims are well-supported by their cited evidence. Tier assignments are appropriate: baseline statistics (E6, E32, E26, E29, E13) are correctly labelled measurable; forward-looking programme targets and projections (E2, E7, E4, E38, E19, E14) are correctly labelled projected. The 'measurable' label on E13 (90,000 social homes consensus) is borderline — it is a research estimate cited via the House of Commons Library — but the quote is accurately represented as a 'consensus' figure, not a hard statistic, so this does not rise to blocking. The RTB claim in E29 covers the 2.02m and 2% replacement figures but the 41% private landlord figure comes from E30; the verdict combines them in one claim citing E29 only — minor provenance gap but not blocking as both come from the same source (blog.anthonycollins.com). Direction 'improves' with moderate magnitude and long-term horizon is well-justified by the evidence. No lever leakage, party bias, or false balance detected. The rationale honestly acknowledges the gap between policy ambition and projected outcomes.

evidence.snippet: Labour commits to the biggest increase in social and affordable housing in a generation. They will strengthen planning obligations for more affordable homes, make changes to the Affordable Homes Programme to deliver more homes from existing funding, and support councils and housing associations to build capacity. New social rented homes will be prioritised, and existing stock better protected by reviewing increased 'right to buy' discounts and increasing protections for newly-built social housing.

sources.quote: Labour will deliver the biggest increase in social and affordable housebuilding in a generation. We will strengthen planning obligations to ensure new developments provide more affordable homes; make changes to the Affordable Homes Programme to ensure that it delivers more homes from existing funding; and support councils and housing associations to build their capacity and make a greater contribution to affordable housing supply. Labour will prioritise the building of new social rented homes and better protect our existing stock by reviewing the increased right to buy discounts introduced in 2012 and increasing protections on newly-built social housing.

evidence.snippet: The current government has pledged to deliver 1.5 million new homes in England across the current Parliament, averaging 300,000 new homes annually.
The new £39 billion Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP), spanning ten years, aims to deliver around 300,000 social and affordable homes, with at least 60% designated for social rent.
This level of funding and targeted delivery is described by the government as the "biggest boost to grant funding in a generation."

However, the Resolution Foundation notes that while delivering 1.5 million new homes would be a "real step-change in housebuilding," it may not be "game-changing" for rebalancing housing supply and demand.
They estimate that 300,000 new homes per year are necessary merely to halt the decline in housing stock relative to the population.
Moreover, the ratio of affordable homes per 1,000 adults in England has consistently fallen since 1980, reaching an all-time low of 88 in 2024.
Even under a best-case scenario, the Resolution Foundation projects the SAHP would only slightly increase this ratio to 91 per 1,000 adults by 2034.
Critics have also warned that the government might struggle to achieve its overall target of 1.5 million new homes.

Strengthen Planning Obligations for More Affordable Homes**
Planning obligations, primarily through Section 106 (S106) agreements, have historically been crucial for delivering affordable homes, accounting for almost half of all new affordable homes over the past decade.
In 2013-14, 16,193 homes were completed through S106, a decrease from over 32,000 in 2006-07.
Changes to planning legislation, such as the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) in 2012, and the use of viability appraisals have allowed developers to reduce affordable housing provision.
The National Housing Federation supports strengthening planning obligations to ensure more affordable homes from new developments.

The House of Commons Library highlights a consensus on the need to build 90,000 social homes annually in England to meet demand, with research suggesting this could generate a net economic benefit of £51.2 billion per year.
However, the IPPR (March 2026) points out that planning reforms have often been "tenure blind," leading councils to approve more market-rate housing rather than social homes.
Issues with build quality and high maintenance costs in some S106 homes have also been noted by housing associations, slowing demand for these properties.

Changes to the Affordable Homes Programme to Deliver More Homes from Existing Funding**
The current Affordable Homes Programme (AHP) 2021-2026 initially received £7.39 billion, with additional injections bringing its total to £8.03 billion, plus a further £2 billion bridge fund (of which Homes England's share is £1.2 billion) to support the transition to the new Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) 2026-2036.
The SAHP, with £39 billion in funding, is intended to deliver approximately 300,000 social and affordable homes over ten years, with a minimum of 60% allocated for social rent.
The Greater London Authority (GLA) also expects to open bidding for the London Social and Affordable Homes Programme 2026-36 in February 2026, targeting at least 60% social rented homes.

While the prioritization of social rent within the AHP guidance is a positive step, cost minimisation rules in Homes England's bids can still inadvertently favour schemes that require less grant, often at the expense of social rented homes which typically need higher grant rates due to lower rental income.

Support Councils and Housing Associations to Build Capacity**
To enhance the capacity of councils and housing associations, the government has launched the Council Housebuilding Skills and Capacity Programme (CHSCP), delivered in partnership with Homes England and the Local Government Association (LGA).
This programme includes a £5.5 million Council Housebuilding Support Fund for 2025-26, designed to help councils more quickly and ambitiously submit bids for the SAHP.
The CHSCP offers tailored support, expert advice, resources, and peer learning, aiming to engage with up to 75 councils during 2025-26.
The Social Housing Bill aims to reduce bureaucracy and provide regulatory certainty to encourage investment in new social and affordable homes.

Additionally, the government has committed £2.5 billion in low-interest loans for Private Registered Providers and extended the "preferential" borrowing rate for council housebuilding from the Public Works Loan Board until March 2027.
The government's Social Housing Renewal Bill and subsequent policy statements confirm this focus.

The new £39 billion SAHP targets at least 60% of its 300,000 homes to be for social rent, a notable shift considering only 14% (75,000) of additional affordable homes in the last decade were social rent.
The Mayor of London's programme shares this 60% social rent target.

However, the continued emphasis on "affordable home ownership" alongside social rent within funding programmes, coupled with cost minimisation rules, could still create tension, potentially hindering the delivery of the most grant-intensive social rented homes, particularly in high-demand areas.

Existing Stock Better Protected by Reviewing Increased 'Right to Buy' Discounts and Increasing Protections for Newly-Built Social Housing**
The Right to Buy (RTB) scheme has significantly depleted social housing stock, with 2.02 million homes sold since 1980, and only 2% replaced in the same period.
Approximately 41% of homes sold through RTB are now in the hands of private landlords.
The UK Housing Review 2022 described RTB as a "strategic failure."
There are currently 1.27 million people on social housing waiting lists and 117,450 households in temporary accommodation.

In response, the government has confirmed sweeping reforms to RTB, including:
*   Increasing the minimum eligibility period from 3 to 10 years.
*   Amending discount rules to a maximum of 15% of the property value (or the cash cap), a significant reduction from previous discounts of 35-70%.
*   Introducing a 35-year new build exemption period, preventing newly built social homes from being sold under RTB for that duration.
*   Exempting homes in designated rural areas and council homes for market rent from RTB.
*   Extending the 'cost floor' protection from 15 to 30 years, ensuring the sale price covers building/maintenance costs.
*   A reduction in maximum cash discounts, implemented in November 2024, is expected to reduce RTB sales by around 25,000 over five years.
While these reforms are welcomed by organisations like the Chartered Institute of Housing (CIH) as a positive step towards addressing the imbalance between homes sold and replaced
, some, including the Housing Forum and Social Housing Action Campaign, advocate for the complete abolition of RTB, following the example of Scotland and Wales.
The National Housing Federation (NHF) also suggested even lower discounts, with a minimum of 0% and a maximum of 5%.
